implementation_notes: Scala's standard library gives every context its own map with the same shape: Option.map applies the function only to a Some (def map[B](f: A => B): Option[B], with the function never evaluated for None), Either is right-biased since 2.12 so map transforms the Right and passes Left through, Try and Future map their success values, and every collection carries map. Future.map is the one that asks for more: it needs an implicit ExecutionContext and runs the function on that executor. Without a typeclass library code can only abstract over a concrete context, because the shared name is a convention rather than an interface; a Functor instance is justified exactly when a function must work for every F[_].
code_sketch:
val host: Option[String] = config.map(_.host)             // None stays None
val port: Either[Error, Int] = parsePort(raw).map(_ + 1)  // Left passes through
val upper: Try[String] = Try(read()).map(_.toUpperCase)

val names = people.map(_.displayName).take(5)             // strict collections
pitfalls: Future.map needs an ExecutionContext in scope and runs the mapping on that executor: a blocking function starves the pool, and failures surface as a failed Future rather than at the call site.
Collection map is strict (one collection per stage) - .view or LazyList is the deferred form - and on Option the type does not reveal whether the function ran.
Either and Try map the success side only (right-bias holds from 2.12): the error channel needs left.map/fold/recover, otherwise error transformations are silently skipped.

variants.name: Cats Functor[F[_]] instance
variants.implementation_notes: Cats provides the operation as an explicit typeclass over any context: trait Functor[F[_]] with def map[A, B](fa: F[A])(f: A => B): F[B], plus lift (turn a plain function into one that maps over F) and a composition instance so F[G[_]] gets a Functor when both do. The typeclass documentation states the laws it must satisfy - identity fa.map(identity) = fa and composition fa.map(f).map(g) = fa.map(g compose f) - which is what lets traverse/sequence, monad transformers and generic libraries be written once against F[_]. Use it when helpers must work across contexts or across types the project does not own; for a single concrete context the stdlib method is shorter and needs no imports.
variants.code_sketch:
import cats.Functor
import cats.syntax.functor._

def addTax[F[_]: Functor](fa: F[Double]): F[Double] = fa.map(_ * 1.19)

addTax(Option(10.0))          // Some(11.9)
addTax(List(1.0, 2.0))        // List(1.19, 2.38)
addTax(Future(3.0))           // needs an implicit ExecutionContext
pitfalls: Instances are resolved implicitly: a missing Functor[F] or an ambiguous custom instance is a compile error pointing at implicit search, not at the map call.
Both the syntax import (cats.syntax.functor._) and the instance scope must be present, otherwise the error is 'value map is not a member of type parameter F[A]'.
Laws stay the author's responsibility: Cats ships law-checking (discipline) precisely because the compiler cannot verify that a hand-written instance is lawful.
